questions.q: What does `systemctl status nginx` show you?
options: Only whether the service is enabled at boot
Whether the service is active, how long it's been running, and its main PID
The full contents of the nginx configuration file
A list of every service currently installed on the system
questions.explain: systemctl status reports the unit's loaded/active state, uptime, and main PID, giving a quick health check for that service.

questions.q: You run `sudo systemctl enable nginx` but do NOT run `start` or use `--now`. What happens?
options: nginx starts running immediately and will also start at every future boot
nginx is NOT running now, but will start automatically at the next boot
Nothing happens at all — enable has no effect without start
nginx starts running now but will not start at the next boot
questions.explain: enable only creates the boot-time symlink; it does not change the service's current running state. start affects the running state; enable affects boot behavior — they're independent.

questions.q: In a systemd unit file, what does `Restart=on-failure` do?
options: Restarts the service every hour on a timer regardless of its state
Automatically restarts the service if it exits with a non-zero (failure) status
Restarts every other service on the system if this one fails
Prevents the service from ever being manually restarted
questions.explain: Restart=on-failure tells systemd to relaunch the unit automatically when its process exits with a failure status, which is the main reason to run long-lived workers as systemd services.

options: They don't actually require sudo on any distribution
They affect system-wide service state, which requires elevated privileges
Only `restart` requires sudo; start and stop do not
sudo is only needed the first time a service is ever started
questions.explain: Starting, stopping, or restarting a systemd-managed service changes system-wide state, so systemd requires root privileges (typically via sudo) to perform these actions.

questions.q: After editing a custom unit file at `/etc/systemd/system/nb-sync.service`, what must you run before the changes take effect?
options: systemctl daemon-reload
Nothing — systemd watches unit files for changes automatically
A full system reboot
systemctl status nb-sync
questions.explain: systemd caches parsed unit files in memory. daemon-reload tells it to re-read unit files from disk so edits take effect before the next start, stop, or restart.
